title: Apple Watch now tracks heart rate continuously
summary: What continuous recording could reveal about arrhythmias, HRV, stress, and recovery.
body_markdown:
It’s rumored that Apple will announce continuous heart rate tracking on Apple Watch, extending measurement beyond workouts into the rest of the day. That could capture a brief racing heart, recovery after stress, or overnight changes.


I worked on the first continuous heart rate tracking app for Apple Watch and coauthored a[JAMA Cardiology study on detecting atrial fibrillation with Apple Watch data](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29562087/) .


There’s a ridiculous amount of signal locked within the humble heart rate sensor: heart rhythm disorders, Long Covid and dysautonomias, HRV, stress, sleep, and fitness.


A[MacRumors forum analysis](https://forums.macrumors.com/threads/watchos-27-hints-at-new-readiness-app-improved-strength-workout-metrics-models-with-new-optical-sensor-family-and-128gb-of-storage.2488563/) reports a new optical-sensing family, **Sunstone 4.0** (` Sunstone4p0` ), alongside the earlier` Sunstone3p75plus` . Our[heart rate accuracy guide](https://www.empirical.health/blog/apple-watch-heart-rate-monitor-accuracy/) traces three optical-sensor generations: the original (2015), Series 4 (2018), and Series 6 (2020). The internal name may hint at revised hardware, but it doesn’t confirm a fourth-generation sensor or continuous background tracking.


## What changes with continuous heart rate tracking?


The 20 examples below span existing uses and research possibilities. More complete recordings could expand them, provided the sensor data and algorithms support each use.


Apple Watch already[records continuously during workouts](https://support.apple.com/en-us/120277) , with intermittent background readings. What additional apps could detect depends on the data Apple provides: beats per minute can show a racing heart; heart rate variability (HRV) requires accurate intervals between beats.


## Heart arrhythmias


**Atrial fibrillation (AFib)** produces an irregular rhythm. Our[JAMA Cardiology study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29562087/) detected AFib from Apple Watch heart rate and step data, performing substantially better in controlled testing than everyday use. Longer recordings could catch intermittent episodes.


**Atrial flutter** can produce a regular pulse, so algorithms that look for irregularity may miss it. Researchers have studied[AFib and flutter detection with wrist optical data](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31689222/) , but confirming the rhythm requires an ECG.


**Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT)** often starts and stops abruptly. Recording when it starts and stops could help a doctor investigate palpitations. A[wearable study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32354450/) found poor performance for short SVT episodes, so the algorithm must also respond fast enough to capture them.


## Does AFib burden predict stroke risk?


**AFib burden is the proportion of monitored time spent in AFib.** Apple’s existing AFib History estimates burden, but[isn’t a continuous monitor](https://www.apple.com/legal/ifu/afhf/1-0/0308/AFHF-IFU-en_US.pdf) .


In[KP-RHYTHM](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamacardiology/fullarticle/2681476) , 1,965 adults with intermittent AFib wore continuous ECG monitors for up to 14 days. Those with AFib/flutter during at least 11.4% of monitored time had **about three times the adjusted rate of thromboembolic events** while off anticoagulants compared with the lower two burden groups (hazard ratio 3.13; 95% CI 1.50–6.56). Events included ischemic stroke, TIA, and other arterial clots.


*Original[KP-RHYTHM Figure 3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6145663/#hoi180020f3) . Unadjusted thromboembolic events per 100 person-years while off anticoagulation, with 95% confidence intervals. AF/flutter burden increases from tertile 1 to 3.*


An[ASSERT analysis](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/38/17/1339/3059370) linked episodes longer than 24 hours to roughly 3.2 times the adjusted risk of stroke or systemic embolism. Neither study establishes a universal safe threshold or validates a smartwatch’s burden estimate.


The randomized[REACT-AF trial](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05836987) is testing continuous anticoagulation against[30-day courses following watch-detected AFib lasting more than an hour](https://reactaf.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/09/REACT-AF-Protocol-Ver-6.0-04-28-2025-Clean.pdf) . An investigational algorithm and supervised protocol will test whether intermittent treatment prevents clots while reducing bleeding. Patients take their prescribed dose during those courses. A low watch-reported burden isn’t a reason to stop prescribed anticoagulation; treatment changes require a clinician’s assessment.


## Long Covid, POTS, and other dysautonomias


Dysautonomias disrupt automatic control of heart rate, blood pressure, and other functions. They can develop after Covid, including postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS).


A heart rate that rises from 70 to 110 after standing and stays there tells a different story from a daily range of 70–110. Pairing continuous readings with posture and symptoms could capture that difference. Evaluating POTS also requires blood pressure measurements, persistent symptoms, and ruling out other causes, as our[active stand test guide](https://www.empirical.health/blog/apple-watch-poor-mans-tilt-test/) explains.


In a[wearable study](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41746-024-01238-x) , the Long Covid group’s average resting heart rate stayed above its pre-infection baseline for 133 days, versus 71 days without Long Covid. Continuous recording could show which activities accompany a racing heart, though a normal trace doesn’t rule out Long Covid.


## How could continuous tracking improve HRV?


Heart rate variability measures changes in the intervals between normal beats. Frequency analysis separates fast fluctuations, such as those with each breath, from slower ones.


*Real ECG-derived beat intervals from[PhysioNet](https://physionet.org/content/nsr2db/1.0.0/) , record nsr001, 00:05–01:05. Red: one hour; tan: its first minute. Logarithmic axes. Data: Phyllis Stein / PhysioNet,[ODC-By 1.0](https://physionet.org/content/nsr2db/view-license/1.0.0/) ; analysis by Empirical Health.*


At 0.25 Hz, a fluctuation repeats every four seconds; at 0.01 Hz, every 100 seconds. The vertical axis shows how much variability occurs around each frequency. Longer recordings resolve slower changes. The curves also differ because physiology changes over the hour and the longer analysis averages multiple windows.


**High-frequency (HF)** variability largely reflects the vagus nerve adjusting heart rate with each breath (parasympathetic activity). **Low-frequency (LF)** variability includes blood-pressure regulation and mixed autonomic influences; it isn’t a direct sympathetic activity meter. The mechanisms behind **very-low-frequency (VLF)** variability are[less settled](https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.14604) ; autonomic, hormonal, and temperature regulation may contribute.


VLF spans roughly 0.0033–0.04 Hz, or cycles lasting 25 seconds to five minutes. An hour captures twelve cycles of a five-minute fluctuation. Continuous beat recording could reveal those patterns; scattered one-minute samples can’t recover the gaps.


HRV analysis must account for motion artifacts and abnormal beats. Recording length also affects SDNN, the HRV metric Apple uses: overnight and brief daytime measurements aren’t interchangeable.


## Can heart rate show stress and recovery?


In a[2022 study](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6579/ac6b7c) , 197 adults took public-speaking and arithmetic stress tests. From arithmetic to recovery, changes in perceived stress correlated with changes in heart rate ( **ρ = 0.268** ) and RMSSD, an HRV measure ( **ρ = −0.213** ), among 185 participants.


A[workday study of 221 adults with overweight and psychological distress](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4620623/) found a similarly modest correlation between perceived stress and an HRV-derived stress index ( **adjusted r = 0.217** ), distinct from Apple’s SDNN metric.


Continuous data could show whether heart rate settles after a difficult meeting. Breathing, heat, and movement also affect heart rate and HRV, so interpreting these modest correlations requires context.


## What could continuous tracking reveal about sleep and fitness?


A[study of 4,098 Finnish employees](https://mental.jmir.org/2018/1/e23/) linked alcohol to higher heart rate and poorer HRV-derived recovery during the first three hours of sleep, with larger changes at higher doses. Continuous tracking could show whether heart rate settles after bedtime or stays elevated for hours.


Apple Watch already records continuously during logged workouts. Continuous background recording could capture an unlogged walk or recovery beyond the workout window. Comparing the same walk over time could show how that response changes.
